whyChoose.title: Why Acting Quickly in California Matters

items.title: The Clock Is Running
items.desc: California generally gives you two years from the date of injury to file a personal injury claim. If a government entity was involved, that window can shrink to as little as six months, so it pays to act early.

items.title: Shared Fault Doesn't Shut You Out
items.desc: California follows pure comparative fault, meaning even if you were partly responsible for what happened, you can still recover damages — just reduced by your share of fault.

items.title: No Cap on Pain and Suffering
items.desc: In ordinary injury cases, California places no cap on non-economic damages like pain and suffering, so your recovery isn't artificially limited by a statutory ceiling.

items.title: No Fee Unless There's a Recovery
items.desc: Attorneys in our network typically work on contingency, which means you generally don't pay unless money is recovered on your behalf.

items.question: How much time do I have to file a claim in California?
items.answer: Generally, you have two years from the date of the injury to file a personal injury lawsuit in California. If your injury involved a government agency or vehicle, that deadline can be as short as six months, so it's worth checking sooner rather than later.

items.question: What if I was partly at fault for the accident?
items.answer: California uses a pure comparative fault rule, which means you can still recover compensation even if you share some blame. Your recovery would simply be reduced by your percentage of fault, not eliminated.

items.question: Where do crashes tend to happen in Crescent City?
items.answer: Based on public-record collision counts, roads like Rt 101, 5th Street, US-101, and L Street show higher reported crash volumes than other local streets. This reflects reporting data only and isn't meant to label any road as unsafe.

items.question: Does LawProactive charge anything to connect me with an attorney?
items.answer: No. LawProactive is a free service, and there's no cost or obligation to see if an independent attorney is a fit for your situation. We are not a law firm and don't handle your case directly.

items.question: Will I have to pay an attorney upfront if I take a case forward?
items.answer: Most attorneys in our network work on a contingency basis, meaning there's typically no fee unless they recover money for you. This lets injured people get help without worrying about upfront legal costs.
